[1] The minnow tanks had been empty since April, but the store still smelled of them, a cold green smell that rose out of the concrete floor whenever the sun reached the front window. My cousin Dell propped the door open with a cinder block the first morning and announced that we would have the place cleared by Friday. He had brought a roll of orange price stickers and a marker, and on the back of an envelope he had already listed what he thought each thing was worth. I had brought coffee. It seemed, even then, a fair summary of the two of us.

[2] Our grandfather had run Pruitt's Bait and Tackle on the north shore of Carrow Lake for forty-four years, and for the last six of them he had run it mostly from a lawn chair behind the counter, telling people where the perch were. When he died in March, the family agreed that Dell and I, the only grandchildren living within a day's drive, would empty the building before the bank listed it. Nobody said aloud that we were also the two who had worked the counter as kids, or that we had hardly spoken since Dell moved to the city and I stayed.

[3] Dell worked the way he did everything, fast and from the outside in. By noon he had stickered every rod on the wall rack and hauled the dead freezer to the curb. I started behind the counter and got almost nowhere. There was a cigar box of hooks sorted by size, with a scrap of paper in each compartment labeled in our grandfather's square capitals. There was a drawer of reading glasses, eleven pairs, left by customers who never came back for them. There was a calendar from 1998 that nobody had taken down because, Dell said, it showed a largemouth bass, and you did not throw away a bass.

[4] "You can't read every label," he said, standing over me around two. "We'll be here till Christmas."

[5] "I'm not reading them. I'm looking at them."

[6] "That's slower."

[7] He was right, and I said so, and that seemed to take something out of him. He sat down on an overturned bucket and drank the coffee I had brought.

[8] The thing neither of us knew what to do with was the board. It hung beside the register, a square of green chalkboard about the size of a pizza box, and on it, in the same square capitals, were names and numbers: HALVORSEN 14. THE TWINS 6.50. RUTH K. 31. There were nineteen names. Every kid who had worked the counter knew what the board meant. If you came up short, you took your bait and your line anyway, and our grandfather chalked you up. When you paid, he wiped your name off with the side of his fist.

[9] "That's about two hundred dollars," Dell said. He had added it in his head. "We could put a notice in the paper. Some of them would pay."

[10] I said I thought some of those names had been up there since we were children. Ruth K., I was nearly sure, had been on the board the summer I was eleven, and the number beside her name had been thirty-one then too.

[11] Dell looked at it for a long time. Then he took out his phone and photographed the board, close up, so that every name could be read, and then again from farther back, so that the picture also held the register and the edge of the window and the empty lawn chair. He did not say what the pictures were for, and I did not ask.

[12] On Friday afternoon, with the rods sold and the shelves bare, a woman in a rain jacket came to the open door and asked whether we were Walt's grandkids. She had a twenty, a ten, and a single folded together in her hand. She was Ruth Kessler, she said, and she had paid that thirty-one dollars in 1994. Our grandfather had taken the money, put it in the register, and left her name exactly where it was. "He said if he wiped me off I'd stop coming in," she said. "He was probably right." She wanted to pay it once more, properly, so that it would be finished.

[13] Dell, who had wanted the place empty by Friday, took the bills, thanked her, and put them in his shirt pocket. Then he walked over to the board, lifted it off its nail, and set it face up in the back seat of his car, on top of his jacket, where nothing would rub against the chalk.
prompt: According to the narrator, the names and numbers on the board beside the register recorded:
choices: amounts that customers had taken in goods and had not yet paid for.
sums that customers had often paid in advance toward their next bait and line.
wages owed to the kids who had worked the counter over the summers.
the prices their grandfather charged his oldest customers for bait.
correct_answer: amounts that customers had taken in goods and had not yet paid for.
explanation: Paragraph 8 explains that if a customer "came up short," they took their bait and line anyway and the grandfather "chalked you up," wiping the name off "When you paid." So each entry was a debt for goods already taken. Money paid in advance would run the opposite way: the name goes up because the customer has not paid. Nothing connects the board to the counter kids' pay; the narrator mentions those kids only as people who knew what it meant. And the numbers are running balances for named people, not a price list.

passage:
[1] Walk into a large public library in the United States today and you may find, somewhere past the new fiction, a shelf of objects that would have puzzled a librarian of fifty years ago: a cordless drill, a ukulele, a telescope, a cake pan shaped like a dinosaur, a box of envelopes holding bean and tomato seeds. These collections go by several names, the most common being a "library of things," and they have spread steadily since the early 2000s. To some patrons they look like a gimmick, a way for an institution worried about its future to seem current. Their history suggests something closer to the opposite.

[2] Tool lending, at least, is not new. Berkeley, California, opened a tool lending library in 1979, and a handful of other cities followed in the decades after. What changed more recently was the range of objects and the reasons offered for them. Seed libraries, which typically let patrons "borrow" seeds in spring and ask them, without enforcing it, to return seeds saved from their own harvest in the fall, spread through public libraries in the years after 2010. Musical instruments, sewing machines, and electronics kits arrived alongside them. The common justification was that many households need such things rarely, and that buying one for each household wastes money and space.

[3] Advocates often support that claim with a striking statistic: that the average household drill is used for only about thirteen minutes in its entire life. The figure is repeated widely, but its origin is hard to trace, and it may be no more than a guess that hardened through repetition. The argument does not need it. It is enough to observe that most people who own a ladder do not use it every week, and that a library has always been, at bottom, an arrangement for sharing things that individuals use occasionally and could not easily afford to own in quantity.

[4] Seen this way, the book itself was once a "thing" in exactly this sense. In the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, when printed books were costly, subscription libraries let members pool their money to buy volumes that few of them could have bought alone. The public library extended that principle to everyone. Books became cheap enough over time that the original economic argument for lending them faded, and libraries justified themselves instead in the language of education and reading. A drill, oddly, returns the institution to its first reason for existing.

[5] None of this makes the new collections easy to run. A book that comes back with a coffee stain can still be read; a drill that comes back with a stripped chuck cannot be used, and someone has to notice. Libraries that lend tools have had to train staff to inspect them, decide who pays for repairs, and write rules about liability that a book collection never required. Seeds raised a different problem. In 2014, agricultural officials in Pennsylvania told one county library that its seed exchange was subject to laws written for commercial seed sellers, which require testing and labeling. Similar questions surfaced in other states, and in the years afterward a number of them changed their rules to exempt noncommercial seed sharing. The episode showed that lending an object can draw an institution into regulations it had never had reason to consider.

[6] The deeper question is whether such collections change what a library is. Critics argue that each drill and ukulele competes for shelf space and staff hours with the reading and research that libraries alone provide, and that an institution which tries to be everything risks being valued for nothing in particular. That worry deserves an answer, and the best one may be that the collections bring in people who would not otherwise have come through the door. A patron who arrives to borrow a sewing machine walks past the books on the way to the desk. Whether that patron ever borrows one is harder to know; few libraries have measured it.

[7] What can be said is that the library of things is less a departure than a reminder. The institution was built on the idea that some goods are better held in common than owned privately, and for a long time the only good it applied that idea to was print. The shelf of drills simply asks which other goods might qualify.

passage_title: Carrying a Joke Across: Two Views
passage:
Passage A

[1] The first joke I ever lost was a pun on the word for "chair." It occurs on page four of a comic novel I was hired to translate, and it depends on the fact that, in the original language, the word for a chair and the word for a seat in parliament are the same. A minor official, newly elected, keeps offering his chair to visitors; the reader laughs because he is also, without meaning to, offering up his office. In English the two meanings have nothing to do with each other. Translated word for word, the passage is a man being oddly polite about furniture.

[2] I spent two days on that page. In the end I did what translators of comedy usually do, though we seldom admit it: I wrote a different joke. My official now keeps insisting that visitors "take a seat," and a few lines later he is horrified to learn that someone else intends to "run for" his. The pun is not the author's, but the laugh lands where hers did, at the same character's expense, for the same reason.

[3] People who have never translated tend to think of this as cheating. I think of it as the only honest choice. A joke is not its words; it is an event that happens in a reader, a small collapse of expectation that takes about a second. If the English reader does not laugh at that moment, I have not preserved the author's sentence. I have preserved its corpse. Fidelity, for comedy, means fidelity to the laugh.

[4] I will grant that the method has a cost. Each substitution moves the book a little farther from its home. Enough of them, and the comic novel becomes a comic novel set nowhere. So I ration them. Where a joke can survive the crossing, even bruised, I let it cross. Where it cannot, I ask a narrower question than "What did the author write?" I ask what the joke was doing: which character it diminished, what it set up for later, how long the reader was meant to keep smiling. Then I write the smallest English joke that does those things, and I keep a list, for the author and for myself, of every one I invented.

Passage B

[1] When I translate a comic writer, I try to keep her jokes, including the ones that will not work in English. This surprises editors, who would rather the book be funny than faithful, and I understand their position. A reader who buys a comic novel expects to laugh, and a translator who strips the laughter out of a funny book has failed it in an obvious way.

[2] But consider what a substituted joke does. It tells the reader that the original humor was the same as ours, only dressed in other words, that a pun about a parliamentary seat is simply a pun, interchangeable with any other. That is rarely true. What a culture finds funny is one of the most specific things about it. A joke that turns on the double meaning of "chair" tells you that, in that place, a political office is imagined as somewhere a person sits, and perhaps refuses to get up from. An English replacement may get its laugh, but it gets it by deleting that piece of information.

[3] So I prefer to let the joke arrive damaged. Sometimes a brief clause can carry the second meaning without stopping the sentence; occasionally a footnote is unavoidable, though a footnote kills a joke as surely as explaining it at a party. Often I simply leave the joke there, unexplained, and trust that a reader who senses something was meant to be funny will be curious rather than cheated.

[4] The reader of a translation should feel, now and then, that the book was written somewhere else. A little bafflement is not a failure of the translation. It is part of what the translation is for. A book that has been made perfectly comfortable in English has been made, in one important sense, into an English book.

[1] For years, residents of the Maldives, a chain of low coral islands in the Indian Ocean, had noticed something odd every autumn. Around October, swarms of dragonflies appeared, sometimes in the thousands, hawking over the beaches and the gardens. The puzzle was where they came from. Dragonflies lay their eggs in fresh water, and their young, called nymphs, live underwater for weeks or months before emerging as winged adults. The Maldives have almost no standing fresh water. The insects could not have hatched there, and the nearest large landmass, India, lies several hundred kilometers away across open sea.

[2] Most of the dragonflies belonged to one species, the globe skimmer, a small amber-colored insect found in warm regions on every continent except Antarctica. A marine biologist working in the islands proposed, in a paper published in 2009, that the globe skimmers were not merely blown off course. He argued that they were making a deliberate crossing from India, riding the winds that shift south across the ocean as the monsoon season ends, and that many continued onward to East Africa. There, the seasonal rains create shallow, temporary pools in which the insects breed. Their offspring, he suggested, would eventually ride the reversed winds of the following season back toward India. If he was right, the full circuit covered more than ten thousand kilometers, farther than any other insect migration then known, and no single dragonfly flew all of it. The journey was relayed across several generations, each completing one leg.

[3] The proposal was bold, and at first it rested mostly on timing: the dragonflies' appearance in the Maldives matched the arrival of the winds that could carry them. Later evidence came from chemistry. The water an insect drinks and lives in as a nymph leaves a signature in its body, because rainwater in different regions contains slightly different proportions of heavy and light forms of hydrogen. That signature stays fixed in the wings once the adult emerges. When researchers analyzed the wings of dragonflies caught in the Maldives, the results pointed to the Indian subcontinent as the place where many had grown up, just as the proposal predicted.

[4] How a creature weighing a fraction of a gram survives such a crossing is a separate question. Part of the answer lies in the globe skimmer's build. Its hind wings are unusually broad at the base, giving it a large wing area for its weight, so that it can glide for long stretches on rising air with very little flapping. Observers have recorded globe skimmers flying a kilometer or more above the ground, high enough to reach fast-moving winds.
